chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: But strangely, all these measures, efforts, and plans—which were no worse than those issued in similar circumstances—had no effect on the real situation. Like the hands of a clock disconnected from the mechanism, they swung about aimlessly without engaging the gears.

Regarding the military plan of campaign—that work of genius which Thiers describes as surpassingly profound, skillful, and admirable (entering into a debate with Fain about whether it should be dated to the fourth or fifteenth of October)—that plan was never and could never be carried out, because it was completely detached from reality. The fortification of the Kremlin, for which the mosque (as Napoleon called the Cathedral of St. Basil) was to have been demolished, proved entirely useless. The mining of the Kremlin only served to fulfill Napoleon's wish to blow it up when he left Moscow—like a child wanting to hit the floor where he hurt himself. The pursuit of the Russian army, which Napoleon fretted over, produced an unheard-of result. The French generals lost track of the Russian army of sixty thousand men, and according to Thiers, it was only found again—like a lost pin—through the skill, and apparently the genius, of Murat.

In diplomacy, all Napoleon's arguments about his magnanimity and justice—to both Tutolmin and Yakovlev (whose main concern was getting a coat and a carriage)—proved useless. Alexander did not receive these envoys and did not reply to their messages.
In legal matters, after the supposed arsonists were executed, the rest of Moscow burned down anyway.

In administrative affairs, the establishment of a municipal government didn't stop the looting. It was only useful to certain people who used their positions to loot Moscow themselves or to protect their own property from being looted.

In religious matters—which Napoleon had handled so easily in Egypt by visiting a mosque—no results were achieved. Two or three priests who were found in Moscow tried to carry out Napoleon's wishes, but one was slapped in the face by a French soldier during a service, and a French official reported of another: "The priest whom I found and invited to say Mass cleaned and locked up the church. That night the doors were broken open again, the padlocks smashed, the books torn up, and other outrages committed."

Regarding trade, the proclamation to industrious workers and peasants got no response. There were no industrious workers to be found, and the peasants caught the officials who ventured too far from town with the proclamation and killed them.

As for the theaters meant to entertain the troops and people, these also failed. The theaters set up in the Kremlin and in Posnyakov's house had to close almost immediately because the actors and actresses were robbed.

Even philanthropy didn't produce the desired effect. The genuine paper money, along with the counterfeit notes that flooded Moscow, all lost their value. The French, focused on collecting loot, wanted only gold. Not only was the paper money Napoleon so generously distributed to the unfortunate worthless, but even silver lost its value relative to gold.
But the most striking example of how ineffective the authorities' orders were at this time was Napoleon's attempt to stop the looting and restore discipline.
Here is what the army authorities were reporting:
"Looting continues in the city despite the decrees against it. Order is not yet restored, and not a single merchant is trading lawfully. Only the sutlers dare to trade, and they sell stolen goods."

"The area around my ward continues to be pillaged by soldiers of the 3rd Corps who, not content with taking from the unfortunate residents hiding in cellars the little they have left, are brutal enough to wound them with their sabers, as I have repeatedly witnessed."
"Nothing new, except that the soldiers continue to rob and loot. October 9."
"Robbery and pillage continue. There is a band of thieves in our district who should be arrested by a strong force. October 11."

"The Emperor is extremely displeased that despite strict orders to stop the pillaging, groups of marauding Guards are constantly seen returning to the Kremlin. Among the Old Guard, disorder and plunder were renewed more violently than ever yesterday evening, last night, and today. The Emperor sees with regret that his handpicked soldiers, who should set an example of discipline, carry disobedience to the point of breaking into cellars and warehouses containing army supplies. Others have gone so far as to defy sentries and officers, and have abused and beaten them."

"The Grand Marshal of the Palace," wrote the governor, "complains bitterly that despite repeated orders, the soldiers continue to relieve themselves in all the courtyards and even beneath the Emperor's own windows."
That army—like a herd of cattle gone wild, trampling the very food that might have saved it from starvation—was disintegrating and perishing with each day it remained in Moscow. But it didn't leave.

It began to flee only when it was suddenly seized by panic over the capture of supply trains on the Smolensk road and the Battle of Tarutino. The news of that battle, unexpectedly reaching Napoleon during a review, stirred in him a desire to punish the Russians (Thiers says), and he issued the departure order the whole army was demanding.

Fleeing from Moscow, the soldiers took everything they'd stolen with them. Napoleon, too, carried off his personal treasure. But seeing the baggage trains clogging the army's movement, he was (Thiers says) horror-struck. Yet with all his war experience, he didn't order the excess vehicles burned, as he had done with a certain marshal's baggage on the approach to Moscow. He looked at the carriages full of soldiers and remarked that it was actually a good thing—those vehicles could be used to carry provisions, the sick, and the wounded.

The whole army's plight resembled that of a wounded animal which senses it is dying and doesn't know what it's doing. Studying the brilliant tactics and aims of Napoleon and his army from their entry into Moscow until their destruction is like studying the dying leaps and convulsions of a mortally wounded creature. Very often a wounded animal, hearing a rustle, charges straight at the hunter's gun, runs forward and back, and hastens its own death. Napoleon, under pressure from his entire army, did the same. The sound of the Battle of Tarutino frightened the beast, and it rushed toward the hunter's gun, reached him, turned back, and finally—like any wild creature—fled along the most dangerous, familiar path where its old scent lingered.

Throughout that entire period, Napoleon—who appears to us to have been the leader of all these events, just as the figurehead of a ship might seem to a primitive observer to steer the vessel—acted like a child holding a couple of strings inside a carriage, imagining he is driving it.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Early in the morning of October sixth, Pierre went out of the shed and, on his way back, stopped by the door to play with a little blue-gray dog with a long body and short, bowed legs that was jumping around him. This little dog lived in their shed, sleeping beside Karataev at night. It sometimes wandered into town but always came back. It had probably never had an owner—it belonged to nobody and had no name. The French called it Azor; the soldier who told stories called it Femgalka; Karataev and the others called it Gray, or sometimes Flabby. Having no master, no name, and not even a definite breed or color didn't seem to bother the blue-gray dog in the least. Its furry tail stood up firm and round like a plume, its crooked little legs served it so well that it would often gracefully lift a hind leg and trot along quickly on three legs, as if disdaining to use all four. Everything pleased it. One moment it would roll on its back yelping with delight, the next it would bask in the sun with an air of self-important thoughtfulness, then frolic around playing with a stick or a piece of straw.

Pierre's outfit now consisted of a dirty, torn shirt (the only remnant of his former clothing), a pair of soldier's trousers that he tied at the ankles with string on Karataev's advice for warmth, and a peasant coat and cap. He had changed a great deal physically. He no longer looked stout, though he still had the solid, strong build that ran in his family. A beard and mustache covered the lower part of his face, and a tangle of hair, infested with lice, curled around his head like a cap. The look in his eyes was resolute, calm, and alertly alive—unlike anything before. The old slackness that had shown even in his eyes was now replaced by an energetic readiness for action and resistance. His feet were bare.

Pierre first looked across the field where vehicles and riders were passing that morning, then into the distance across the river, then at the dog pretending to seriously bite him, and then down at his own bare feet, which he placed in various positions with obvious pleasure, wiggling his dirty, thick big toes. Every time he looked at his bare feet, a smile of amused self-satisfaction crossed his face. The sight of them reminded him of everything he had experienced and learned during these weeks, and the memory was pleasant.
For several days the weather had been calm and clear, with slight frosts in the morning—what people call an 'old wives' summer.'
In the sunshine the air was warm, and that warmth was especially pleasant alongside the invigorating freshness of the morning frost still lingering in the air.

On everything near and far lay that magical crystal shimmer you see only in autumn. The Sparrow Hills were visible in the distance—the village, the church, the large white house. The bare trees, the sand, the bricks and rooftops, the green church spire, and the corners of the white house all stood out in the transparent air with an unnaturally delicate clarity. Nearby were the familiar ruins of a half-burned mansion occupied by the French, with lilac bushes still showing dark green beside the fence. Even that ruined, defiled house—repulsively ugly in dull weather—looked quietly beautiful now in the clear, motionless light.
A French corporal, his coat unbuttoned in a homey way, a skullcap on his head and a short pipe in his mouth, came around the corner of the shed and approached Pierre with a friendly wink.
'What sunshine, Monsieur Kiril!' (That was their name for Pierre.) 'Just like spring!'
And the corporal leaned against the door and offered Pierre his pipe, though Pierre always declined it.
'To be on the march in such weather...' he began.

Pierre asked what was being said about leaving, and the corporal told him that nearly all the troops were departing and there should be orders about the prisoners that day. Sokolov, one of the soldiers sharing Pierre's shed, was dying, and Pierre told the corporal that something should be done about him. The corporal replied that Pierre needn't worry—they had an ambulance and a hospital, and arrangements would be made for the sick. In general, everything that could happen had been anticipated by the authorities.

'Besides, Monsieur Kiril, you only have to say a word to the captain, you know. He's a man who never forgets anything. Have a word with the captain when he makes his rounds—he'll do anything for you.'
(The captain the corporal mentioned often had long conversations with Pierre and showed him all kinds of favors.)

'"You see, St. Thomas," he said to me the other day, "Monsieur Kiril is an educated man who speaks French. He's a Russian gentleman who's had bad luck, but he's a real man. He knows what's what. If he needs anything and asks me, he won't be refused. When a man has had an education, you see, he appreciates learning and well-bred people." I mention this for your sake, Monsieur Kiril. The other day, if it hadn't been for you, that business would have ended badly.'

After chatting a while longer, the corporal went away. (The incident he'd mentioned had happened a few days earlier—a fight between the prisoners and the French soldiers, in which Pierre had managed to calm his comrades down.) Some prisoners who had overheard Pierre talking to the corporal immediately asked what the Frenchman had said. While Pierre was relaying the news about the army leaving Moscow, a thin, sallow, ragged French soldier came to the shed door. Quickly and timidly raising his fingers to his forehead in greeting, he asked Pierre whether the soldier Platoche—to whom he had given a shirt to sew—was in this shed.
A week earlier, the French had been issued boot leather and linen, which they'd given to the prisoners to make into boots and shirts.
'Ready, ready, my friend!' said Karataev, coming out with a neatly folded shirt.

Karataev, because of the warm weather and for ease of work, was wearing only trousers and a tattered shirt as black as soot. His hair was tied up workman-style with a strip of lime bark, and his round face looked rounder and more pleasant than ever.
'A promise is a sacred thing! I said Friday, and here it is—ready,' said Platon, smiling as he unfolded the shirt he had sewn.

The Frenchman glanced around nervously, then, as if overcoming his hesitation, quickly pulled off his uniform and put on the shirt. Under the uniform, next to his sallow, thin bare body, he wore a long, greasy, flowered silk waistcoat—but no shirt. He was clearly afraid the watching prisoners would laugh at him, and thrust his head into the shirt quickly. None of the prisoners said a word.
'See, it fits nicely!' Platon kept saying, smoothing the shirt straight.
The Frenchman pushed his head and hands through without looking up, examining the shirt and checking the seams.

'You know, my friend, this isn't a tailor's shop, and I didn't have the right tools. As they say, you need the proper tool even to crack a louse,' said Platon with one of his warm, round smiles, clearly pleased with his work.
'It's good, quite good, thank you,' said the Frenchman in French, 'but there must be some fabric left over.'
'It'll fit even better once it settles to your body,' said Karataev, still admiring his handiwork. 'You'll be nice and comfortable...'
'Thanks, thanks, old fellow... But the leftover pieces?' the Frenchman said again, smiling. He took out a ruble note and gave it to Karataev. 'But give me the scraps that are left.'

Pierre saw that Platon didn't want to understand what the Frenchman was saying, and he watched without interfering. Karataev thanked the Frenchman for the money and went on admiring his own work. The Frenchman insisted on getting back the leftover material and asked Pierre to translate.
'What does he want the scraps for?' said Karataev. 'They'd make fine leg wrappings for us. Well, never mind.'

And Karataev, his face suddenly changed and saddened, took a small bundle of scraps from inside his shirt and handed it to the Frenchman without looking at him. 'Oh well!' he muttered, and walked away. The Frenchman looked at the cloth, thought for a moment, then glanced inquiringly at Pierre and—as if Pierre's expression told him something—suddenly blushed and shouted in a squeaky voice:
'Platoche! Hey, Platoche! Keep them yourself!' And handing back the scraps, he turned and walked out.

'There, look at that,' said Karataev, shaking his head. 'People said they weren't Christians, but they have souls too. It's what the old folks used to say: "A sweating hand is an open hand, a dry hand is a tight one." He's got nothing himself, but he gave them back.'
Karataev smiled thoughtfully and sat quietly for a while, looking at the pieces of cloth.
'But they'll make wonderful leg wrappings, my friend,' he said, and went back into the shed.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Four weeks had passed since Pierre had been taken prisoner. Though the French had offered to transfer him from the soldiers' shed to the officers' quarters, he had stayed in the shed where he'd first been placed.

In burned and devastated Moscow, Pierre experienced nearly the furthest limits of deprivation a person can endure. But thanks to his physical strength and health—which he'd been unaware of until now—and especially because the hardships came so gradually that it was impossible to say when they began, he bore his situation not only easily but even joyfully. And it was precisely now that he found the peace of mind and inner harmony he had previously strived for in vain. He had long sought it in different ways—in philanthropy, in Freemasonry, in the distractions of city life, in wine, in heroic self-sacrifice, and in his romantic love for Natasha. He had sought it through reason—and all these attempts had failed him. Now, without thinking about it, he had found that peace and inner harmony only through the horror of death, through deprivation, and through what he recognized in Karataev.

Those terrible moments he had lived through at the executions had washed away from his mind, as if forever, the anxious thoughts and feelings that had once seemed so important. It no longer occurred to him to think about Russia, or the war, or politics, or Napoleon. It was obvious to him that none of these were his concern, that he had no business judging them, and therefore couldn't. 'Russia and summer weather don't come tied together,' he thought, repeating Karataev's words, which he found strangely comforting. His intention of killing Napoleon and his calculations about the number of the Beast in Revelation now seemed meaningless and even ridiculous. His anger at his wife, his worry about his name being dishonored—these seemed not just trivial but amusing. What did it matter to him that some woman somewhere was living as she pleased? What did it matter to anyone, especially him, whether they discovered that their prisoner's name was Count Bezukhov?

He now often recalled his conversation with Prince Andrew and completely agreed with him, though he understood Andrew's thoughts somewhat differently. Prince Andrew had said that happiness could only be negative, but he'd said it with a shade of bitterness and irony, as though he were really saying that the desire for positive happiness is planted in us only to torment us and never be satisfied. But Pierre believed this without any mental reservation. The absence of suffering, the satisfaction of one's needs, and the consequent freedom to choose one's occupation—that is, one's way of life—now seemed to Pierre to be unquestionably the highest human happiness. Here and now, for the first time, he fully appreciated the pleasure of eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, sleeping when tired, warmth when cold, and talking to another person when he wanted to hear a human voice. The satisfaction of one's needs—good food, cleanliness, freedom—now that he was deprived of all this, seemed to Pierre to constitute perfect happiness. And the choice of occupation—now that this was so restricted—seemed such a simple matter that he forgot how an excess of life's comforts destroys the joy of meeting one's needs, and how great freedom in choosing one's path—the kind his wealth, education, and social position had given him—is exactly what makes that choice impossibly difficult and kills the desire and ability to have any occupation at all.

All Pierre's daydreams now centered on the time when he would be free. Yet for the rest of his life, he thought and spoke with deep feeling about that month of captivity—those irretrievable, powerful, joyful sensations, and above all the complete peace of mind and inner freedom he experienced only during those weeks.

When on the first day he rose early, stepped out of the shed at dawn, and saw the domes and crosses of the New Convent of the Virgin still dark against the sky, the hoarfrost on the dusty grass, the Sparrow Hills, and the wooded banks above the winding river fading into the purple distance; when he felt the touch of fresh air and heard the crows flying from Moscow across the field; and when light flared from the east and the sun's rim appeared solemnly from behind a cloud, and the domes and crosses, the frost, the distance, and the river all began to sparkle in the joyful light—Pierre felt a new strength and joy in life such as he had never known. And this feeling not only stayed with him throughout his imprisonment but even grew stronger as his hardships increased.

That alertness and readiness for anything was further strengthened by the high opinion his fellow prisoners formed of him soon after his arrival. His knowledge of languages, the respect the French showed him, his simplicity, his willingness to give away anything asked of him (he received the officers' allowance of three rubles a week), his strength (which he demonstrated by pressing nails into the hut's walls), his gentleness toward his companions, and his ability to sit still and think without doing anything (which struck them as mysterious)—all this gave him an almost heroic status among them. The very qualities that had been a hindrance, even harmful, in his former world—his strength, his indifference to comfort, his absent-mindedness and simplicity—here, among these people, made him nearly a hero. And Pierre felt that their opinion placed responsibilities on him.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: The French evacuation began on the night between the sixth and seventh of October: kitchens and sheds were dismantled, carts loaded, and troops and baggage trains set off.

At seven in the morning, a French convoy in marching order—wearing shakos and carrying muskets, knapsacks, and enormous sacks—stood in front of the sheds. Animated French conversation mixed with curses sounded along the entire line.

In the shed, everyone was ready—dressed, belted, and wearing shoes—waiting only for the order to start. Only the sick soldier Sokolov, pale and thin with dark circles under his eyes, sat barefoot and undressed in his place. His eyes, prominent from the thinness of his face, gazed questioningly at his comrades, who paid no attention to him. He moaned regularly and quietly. It was clearly not so much his suffering that made him moan (he had dysentery) as his fear and grief at being left behind.
Pierre, with a rope tied around his waist and wearing shoes Karataev had made him from leather torn off a tea chest by a French soldier, went up to the sick man and crouched beside him.
"You know, Sokolov, they're not all leaving. There's a hospital here. You might actually be better off than the rest of us," said Pierre.
"Oh Lord! Oh, it'll be the death of me! Oh Lord!" the man moaned louder.
"I'll go ask them again right now," said Pierre, standing up and going to the shed door.

Just as Pierre reached the door, the corporal who had offered him a pipe the day before came up with two soldiers. The corporal and soldiers were in marching gear—knapsacks and shakos with metal chin straps—and these accessories made their familiar faces look completely different.
The corporal had come, on orders, to shut the door. The prisoners had to be counted before being let out.
"Corporal, what will they do with the sick man?..." Pierre began.

But even as he spoke, he began to doubt whether this was really the corporal he knew, or a stranger—so unlike himself did the man seem at that moment. Moreover, just as Pierre spoke, a sharp rattle of drums suddenly burst out from both sides. The corporal frowned at Pierre's words and, muttering some meaningless oaths, slammed the door shut. The shed went dark, and the sharp drum rattle drowned out the sick man's groans from both sides.

"There it is!... That force again!..." Pierre said to himself, and an involuntary shudder ran down his spine. In the corporal's transformed face, in the sound of his voice, in the stirring, deafening noise of the drums, Pierre recognized that mysterious, cold force that compelled people against their will to kill their fellow men—the force he had witnessed during the executions. To fear it, to try to escape it, to plead with or preach to those who served as its instruments was useless. Pierre understood this now. One could only wait and endure. He didn't go back to the sick man or turn to look at him, but stood frowning by the shed door.

When the door was opened and the prisoners, pressing against one another like a flock of sheep, squeezed through the exit, Pierre pushed forward and approached the very captain whom the corporal had assured him would do anything for him. The captain was also in marching gear, and on his cold face Pierre recognized that same force he had seen in the corporal's words and in the roll of the drums.
"Move along, move along!" the captain repeated, frowning sternly and scanning the prisoners streaming past him.
Pierre went up to him, though he knew the attempt would be useless.
"What is it?" the officer asked coldly, as if not recognizing Pierre.
Pierre told him about the sick man.
"He can walk, damn him!" said the captain. "Move along, move along!" he continued without looking at Pierre.
"But he's dying," Pierre began again.
"Would you be so good as to—" the captain shouted, his face darkening with anger.
"Drum-da-da-dum, dum-dum..." rattled the drums, and Pierre understood that this mysterious force had total control over these men and that there was no point saying anything more.
The officer prisoners were separated from the soldiers and told to march in front. There were about thirty officers, Pierre among them, and about three hundred soldiers.

The officers, who had come from other sheds, were all strangers to Pierre and much better dressed. They looked at him and his shoes with suspicion, as if he were an outsider. Not far from him walked a fat major with a sallow, bloated, angry face, wearing a Kazan dressing gown tied with a towel. He clearly commanded respect among his fellow prisoners. He kept one hand, clutching his tobacco pouch, inside the front of his dressing gown and held the stem of his pipe firmly with the other. Panting and puffing, the major grumbled at everyone, convinced he was being pushed and that they were all hurrying for no reason and amazed at nothing worth being amazed about. Another man, a thin little officer, talked to everyone, speculating about where they were being taken and how far they'd march that day. An official in felt boots and a commissariat uniform ran from side to side, pointing at the ruins of Moscow and loudly announcing what had burned and identifying different parts of the city. A third officer, a Pole by his accent, argued with the commissariat man about which neighborhood was which.

"What's the point of arguing?" said the major angrily. "What does it matter if it's St. Nicholas or St. Blaise? It's burned down, and that's the end of it. What are you pushing for? Isn't the road wide enough?" he snapped at someone behind him who wasn't pushing at all.

"Oh, oh, oh! Look what they've done!" the prisoners murmured on all sides, gazing at the charred ruins. "Everything beyond the river, and Zubovo, and the Kremlin... Just look! Not half of it left. Yes, I told you—the whole district beyond the river. That's how it is."
"Well, you can see it's burned. What's the use of talking about it?" said the major.
As they passed a church in the Khamovniki district—one of the few unburned parts of Moscow—the whole crowd of prisoners suddenly recoiled, and exclamations of horror and disgust were heard.
"Oh, the monsters! What heathens! Yes—dead, dead he is... And his face is smeared with something!"

Pierre pushed forward toward the church where this sight was causing such outrage, and dimly made out something propped against the fence around the churchyard. From his companions who could see better, he learned it was a dead body, set upright against the railings with its face smeared with soot.
"Move on! What the devil... Move on! Thirty thousand devils!..." the guards cursed, and the French soldiers drove the crowd of staring prisoners away with fresh viciousness, swords in hand.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Through the side streets of the Khamovniki district, the prisoners marched with only their escort and its vehicles behind them. But when they reached the supply depot, they found themselves engulfed in a massive, tightly packed train of artillery mixed with private carriages.

At the bridge, everyone halted, waiting for those ahead to cross. From the bridge they could see endless lines of moving baggage trains stretching before and behind them. To the right, where the Kaluga road turns near Neskuchny, endless rows of troops and carts disappeared into the distance. These were Beauharnais's troops, who had departed before anyone else. Behind them, along the riverbank and across the Stone Bridge, came Ney's troops and transport.

Davout's forces, who were in charge of the prisoners, were crossing the Crimean Bridge, and some were already turning onto the Kaluga road. But the baggage trains stretched out so far that the last of Beauharnais's column hadn't yet left Moscow and reached the Kaluga road when Ney's vanguard was already emerging from Great Ordynka Street.

After crossing the Crimean Bridge, the prisoners moved a few steps forward, stopped, and moved again. From all sides, vehicles and men pressed closer and closer together. They covered the few hundred yards between the bridge and the Kaluga road in over an hour and emerged onto the square where the streets of the Transmoskva district and the Kaluga road converge. There, jammed tightly together, the prisoners had to stand for hours at the crossroads. From all sides, like the roar of the sea, came the rattle of wheels, the tramp of feet, and incessant shouts of anger and abuse. Pierre stood pressed against the wall of a charred house, listening to this noise, which in his imagination blended with the roll of the drums.
To get a better view, several officer prisoners climbed onto the wall of the half-burned house Pierre was leaning against.

"Look at the crowds! Just look at those crowds! They've loaded goods even onto the cannons! Look—those are furs!" they exclaimed. "Just see what the scoundrels have looted! Look at what that one's got piled behind his cart! Those are icon settings, by God! Oh, the thieves! See how that fellow's weighed down—he can barely walk! Good lord, they've even taken the carriages! Look at that man sitting on the trunks! Heavens—they're fighting!"

"That's right, smack him on the nose! Like this, we won't get out of here before dark. Look, look... That must be Napoleon's own carriage. See those horses! And the monograms with a crown! It's like a house on wheels! That fellow dropped his sack and doesn't even notice. Fighting again... A woman with a baby—and not bad-looking either! Yes, sure, as if they'll let you through... Just look, there's no end to it. Russian girls, by God, that's what they are! Riding in carriages—see how comfortably they've settled in!"

Again, as at the church in Khamovniki, a wave of curiosity swept all the prisoners forward onto the road. Pierre, thanks to his height, could see over the others' heads what had caught their attention. In three carriages wedged among the ammunition carts sat women with rouged faces and garish clothes, shouting something in shrill voices.

From the moment Pierre had recognized that mysterious force, nothing seemed strange or terrible to him anymore—not the soot-smeared corpse, not these women hurrying past, not the burned ruins of Moscow. All that he now witnessed barely made an impression, as if his soul, preparing itself for a hard struggle, refused to take in anything that might weaken it.
The women's carriages passed. Behind them came more carts, soldiers, wagons, soldiers, gun carriages, carriages, soldiers, ammunition carts, more soldiers, and now and then women.
Pierre no longer saw individuals. He saw only their movement.

All these people and horses seemed driven forward by some invisible power. During the hour Pierre watched them, they all flowed from different streets with one and the same desire: to move forward as quickly as possible. They jostled one another, grew angry, fought. White teeth flashed, brows furrowed. The same words of abuse flew from side to side, and every face bore that same expression of swaggering determination and cold cruelty that had struck Pierre that morning in the corporal's face when the drums were beating.

It wasn't until nearly evening that the escort commander collected his men and, with shouts and arguments, forced his way into the baggage train. The prisoners, hemmed in on all sides, emerged onto the Kaluga road.

They marched very quickly without stopping, and halted only when the sun began to set. The baggage carts drew close together and the men began preparing for the night. Everyone seemed angry and dissatisfied. For a long time, curses, furious shouts, and fighting could be heard on all sides. A carriage following the escort collided with one of the carts, punching a hole in it with its shaft. Several soldiers ran toward the cart from different directions: some beat the carriage horses on the head, turning them aside; others fought among themselves. Pierre saw one German badly wounded in the head by a sword.

It seemed that all these men, now stopped in the fields in the chill dusk of an autumn evening, shared one feeling: an unpleasant awakening from the frantic rush to push forward that had seized them at the start. Once standing still, they all seemed to realize they didn't yet know where they were going, and that much that was painful and difficult lay ahead on this journey.
During this halt, the escort treated the prisoners even worse than at the start. For the first time, the prisoners were given horsemeat as their meat ration.
From the officers down to the lowest soldiers, they showed what seemed like personal spite toward each prisoner—in unexpected contrast to their formerly friendly manner.

This hostility increased when, during the roll call, it was discovered that in the chaos of leaving Moscow, one Russian soldier who had pretended to have stomach cramps had escaped. Pierre saw a Frenchman savagely beat a Russian soldier for straying too far from the road, and heard his friend the captain threaten to court-martial a noncommissioned officer over the escape. To the NCO's excuse that the prisoner was sick and couldn't walk, the officer replied that the order was to shoot those who fell behind. Pierre felt that fatal force, which had crushed him during the executions but which he hadn't felt during his imprisonment, once again controlling his existence. It was terrible. But he felt that in proportion to the efforts of that fatal force to crush him, a power of life independent of it was growing and strengthening in his soul.
He ate his supper of buckwheat soup with horsemeat and chatted with his companions.

Neither Pierre nor any of the others spoke about what they'd seen in Moscow, or the rough treatment by the French, or the order to shoot stragglers that had been announced. As if reacting against their worsening situation, they were all particularly lively and cheerful. They talked about personal memories and funny scenes from the campaign, carefully avoiding any mention of their current predicament.

The sun had set long ago. Bright stars appeared here and there in the sky. A red glow like a fire spread above the horizon from the rising full moon, and that vast red ball swayed strangely in the gray haze. It grew light. The evening was ending, but night hadn't come yet. Pierre got up and left his new companions, crossing between the campfires to the other side of the road where the common soldiers' prisoners were quartered. He wanted to talk to them. On the road, a French sentry stopped him and ordered him back.

Pierre turned back—not to his companions by the campfire but to an unhitched cart where nobody was. Tucking his legs under him and lowering his head, he sat down on the cold ground by the wheel and stayed motionless for a long time, deep in thought. Suddenly he burst into a fit of his broad, good-natured laughter—so loud that people on all sides turned in surprise to see what this strange, solitary laughter meant.

"Ha-ha-ha!" laughed Pierre. And he said aloud to himself: "The soldier wouldn't let me pass. They took me and locked me up. They hold me captive. Who—me? Me? My immortal soul? Ha-ha-ha! Ha-ha-ha!..." And he laughed until tears came to his eyes.
A man got up and came over to see what this big, odd fellow was laughing about all by himself. Pierre stopped laughing, got up, moved farther from the curious man, and looked around.

The huge, endless bivouac that had previously echoed with crackling campfires and the voices of many men had grown quiet. The red fires were fading and dying down. High up in the bright sky hung the full moon. Forests and fields beyond the camp, invisible before, now stretched into the distance. And farther still, beyond those forests and fields, the bright, shimmering, limitless distance beckoned. Pierre looked up at the sky and the twinkling stars in their faraway depths. "And all of that is me, all of that is within me, and all of that is what I am!" thought Pierre. "And they caught all that and locked it in a shed boarded up with planks!" He smiled, and went to lie down to sleep beside his companions.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: In the early days of October, another envoy came to Kutuzov with a letter from Napoleon proposing peace, falsely dated from Moscow, though Napoleon was already not far from Kutuzov on the old Kaluga road. Kutuzov replied as he had to Lauriston's earlier letter, saying there could be no question of peace.

Soon after, a report came in from Dorokhov's guerrilla detachment, operating to the left of Tarutino, that troops from Broussier's division had been spotted at Forminsk and, being separated from the main French army, could easily be destroyed. The soldiers and officers again demanded action. Generals on the staff, emboldened by the easy victory at Tarutino, urged Kutuzov to follow Dorokhov's suggestion. Kutuzov didn't think any offensive was necessary. The result was an inevitable compromise: a small detachment was sent to Forminsk to attack Broussier.

By a strange coincidence, this task—which turned out to be one of the most difficult and important of the campaign—was given to Dokhturov, that same modest little Dokhturov whom no one has ever described drawing up battle plans, charging in front of regiments, or showering decorations on batteries, and who was considered and spoken of as indecisive and lacking insight. Yet we find him in command at the most critical position in every engagement of the Russo-French wars from Austerlitz to 1813. At Austerlitz he was the last to hold the Augezd dam, rallying regiments and saving what he could when everyone was fleeing and not a single general remained in the rear guard. Ill with fever, he went to Smolensk with twenty thousand men to defend it against Napoleon's entire army. At the Malakhov Gate in Smolensk, he had barely dozed off in a bout of fever before being woken by the bombardment—and Smolensk held out all day. At Borodino, when Bagration was killed and nine-tenths of the men on the left flank had fallen and the full force of French artillery was directed there, the man sent to that spot was this same 'irresolute and unperceptive' Dokhturov—Kutuzov rushing to correct a mistake he'd made by first sending someone else. And the quiet little Dokhturov rode there, and Borodino became the greatest glory of the Russian army. Many heroes of that time have been celebrated in verse and prose, but about Dokhturov, scarcely a word has been said.

It was Dokhturov again who was sent to Forminsk and from there to Malo-Yaroslavets—the site of the last battle with the French, where the obvious disintegration of the French army began. We hear about many geniuses and heroes of that campaign, but about Dokhturov, nothing or almost nothing, and even that is said doubtfully. This silence about Dokhturov is the clearest proof of his merit.

It's natural for someone who doesn't understand how a machine works to assume that a wood shaving that has accidentally fallen into it and is bouncing around, interfering with its operation, must be its most important part. Someone who doesn't understand the machine's construction can't grasp that the small connecting cog, turning quietly, is one of the most essential parts—not the shaving that merely damages and hinders it.

On October tenth, Dokhturov had gotten halfway to Forminsk and stopped at the village of Aristovo, faithfully preparing to carry out his orders. Then the entire French army—having lurched convulsively toward Murat's position as if to give battle—suddenly and for no apparent reason veered left onto the new Kaluga road and began pouring into Forminsk, where previously only Broussier had been. At that point, Dokhturov had under his command, besides Dorokhov's detachment, the two small guerrilla bands of Figner and Seslavin.

On the evening of October eleventh, Seslavin arrived at Aristovo headquarters with a captured French guardsman. The prisoner said the troops entering Forminsk that day were the vanguard of the entire army—Napoleon was there, and the whole army had left Moscow four days earlier. That same evening, a house servant from Borovsk said he'd seen an enormous army entering the town. Cossacks from Dokhturov's detachment reported sighting the French Guards marching toward Borovsk. From all these reports, it was clear that where they had expected to find a single division, they now faced the entire French army, marching from Moscow in an unexpected direction along the Kaluga road. Dokhturov was unwilling to act, as it was no longer clear what he should do. He'd been ordered to attack Forminsk, but at that time only Broussier had been there—now the whole French army was there. Ermolov wanted to act on his own judgment, but Dokhturov insisted on getting instructions from Kutuzov. So it was decided to send a dispatch to the staff.

For this mission, they chose a capable officer named Bolkhovitinov, who was to explain the situation verbally as well as deliver a written report. Toward midnight, Bolkhovitinov received the dispatch and verbal instructions and galloped off to General Staff headquarters, accompanied by a Cossack with spare horses.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: It was a warm, dark autumn night. It had been raining for four days. Having changed horses twice and galloped twenty miles in an hour and a half over a sticky, muddy road, Bolkhovitinov reached Litashevka after one in the morning. Dismounting at a cottage on whose wattle fence hung a sign reading GENERAL STAFF, he threw down his reins and entered a dark corridor.
"The general on duty—quickly! It's very important!" he said to someone who had risen and was sniffing in the dark passage.
"He's been very unwell since this evening, and this is the third night he hasn't slept," the orderly whispered pleadingly. "You should wake the captain first."
"But this is very important—from General Dokhturov," said Bolkhovitinov, finding the open door by feeling in the dark.
The orderly went in ahead and began waking someone.
"Your honor! Your honor! A courier!"
"What? What's that? From whom?" came a sleepy voice.
"From Dokhturov and Alexei Petrovich. Napoleon is at Forminsk," said Bolkhovitinov, unable to see who was speaking in the dark but guessing from the voice that it wasn't Konovnitsyn.
The man who had been woken yawned and stretched.
"I don't like waking him," he said, fumbling for something. "He's very ill. Maybe this is just a rumor."
"Here's the dispatch," said Bolkhovitinov. "My orders are to deliver it immediately to the general on duty."

"Wait a moment, I'll light a candle. Where do you always hide the damn thing, you rascal?" said the voice of the stretching man to the orderly. (This was Shcherbinin, Konovnitsyn's adjutant.) "I've found it, I've found it!" he added.
The orderly was striking a light, and Shcherbinin was fumbling for the candlestick.
"Oh, the disgusting creatures!" he said with revulsion.
By the light of the sparks, Bolkhovitinov saw Shcherbinin's youthful face as he held the candle, and the face of another man still asleep. This was Konovnitsyn.

When the flame of the sulfur splinter, kindled by the tinderbox, flared first blue then red, Shcherbinin lit the tallow candle—from which cockroaches that had been gnawing on it scurried away—and looked at the messenger. Bolkhovitinov was splattered all over with mud and had smeared his face by wiping it with his sleeve.
"Who sent the report?" asked Shcherbinin, taking the envelope.
"The intelligence is reliable," said Bolkhovitinov. "Prisoners, Cossacks, and scouts all confirm the same thing."

"There's nothing for it—we'll have to wake him," said Shcherbinin, rising and walking over to the man in the nightcap who lay covered by a greatcoat. "Pyotr Petrovich!" he said. (Konovnitsyn didn't stir.) "To the General Staff!" he said with a smile, knowing those words were sure to rouse him.

And indeed, the head in the nightcap lifted at once. On Konovnitsyn's handsome, resolute face, with cheeks flushed from fever, there lingered for a moment a faraway, dreamy expression—then he suddenly snapped to attention, and his face took on its usual calm, firm look.
"Well, what is it? From whom?" he asked immediately, without hurry, blinking at the light.

While listening to the officer's report, Konovnitsyn broke the seal and read the dispatch. He had barely finished before he lowered his legs in their woolen stockings to the dirt floor and began pulling on his boots. Then he took off his nightcap, combed his hair over his temples, and put on his cap.
"Did you get here quickly? Let's go to His Highness."

Konovnitsyn had understood at once that this news was of great importance and that there was no time to lose. He didn't pause to consider whether it was good news or bad. That didn't interest him. He viewed the entire business of the war not through intelligence or reason but through something deeper. Within him lay a deep, unspoken conviction that all would be well—but that one must not rely on this, much less talk about it. One must simply attend to one's own work. And he did his work, giving it his full strength.

Pyotr Petrovich Konovnitsyn, like Dokhturov, seems to have been included merely for form's sake in the list of the so-called heroes of 1812—the Barclays, Raevskys, Ermolovs, Platovs, and Miloradoviches. Like Dokhturov, he had the reputation of being a man of very limited abilities, and like Dokhturov, he never drew up battle plans but was always found where things were most difficult. Since his appointment as general on duty, he always slept with his door open, with orders that every messenger be allowed to wake him. In battle he was always under fire, so that Kutuzov reproached him for it and was afraid to send him to the front. And like Dokhturov, he was one of those unnoticed cogs that, without noise or fuss, form the most essential parts of the machine.

Emerging from the hut into the damp, dark night, Konovnitsyn frowned—partly from a worsening pain in his head and partly at the unpleasant thought of how all those influential men on the staff would be stirred up by this news, especially Bennigsen, who had been at war with Kutuzov ever since Tarutino. He could already picture their suggestions, their quarrels, their orders and counter-orders. This prospect was disagreeable, though he knew it couldn't be avoided.

And indeed, Toll—the first person he went to with the news—immediately began laying out his plans to a general sharing his quarters, until Konovnitsyn, who had been listening in weary silence, reminded him that they needed to go see His Highness.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Kutuzov, like all old people, slept very little at night. He often dropped off unexpectedly during the day, but at night, lying on his bed fully clothed, he generally stayed awake thinking.
So he lay now on his bed, resting his large, heavy, scarred head on his plump hand, with his one good eye open, pondering and peering into the darkness.

Since Bennigsen—who corresponded with the Emperor and held more influence than anyone else on the staff—had begun avoiding him, Kutuzov felt more at ease about the possibility of himself and his troops being forced into useless offensive operations. The lesson of the Battle of Tarutino and the day before it, which Kutuzov remembered with pain, must, he thought, have some effect on others too.

"They must understand that we can only lose by attacking. Patience and time are my warriors, my champions," thought Kutuzov. He knew that you shouldn't pick an apple while it's still green. It will fall by itself when ripe. But if you pick it unripe, you ruin the apple, damage the tree, and set your teeth on edge. Like an experienced hunter, he knew the beast was wounded—wounded as only the combined strength of Russia could have wounded it. But whether the wound was mortal remained an open question. Now, from the fact that Lauriston and Barthélemi had been sent, and from the guerrillas' reports, Kutuzov was almost sure the wound was fatal. But he needed more proof, and he had to wait.

"They want to run over and see how badly they've hurt it. Wait, and we'll see! All these maneuvers, all these advances!" he thought. "What for? Only to make themselves look good. As if fighting were some kind of game. They're like children who can't give you a sensible account of what happened because they all want to show how well they can fight. But that's not what's needed now."

"And what elaborate maneuvers they all propose to me! They seem to think that when they've considered two or three possibilities"—he recalled the general plan sent from Petersburg—"they've thought of everything. But the possibilities are endless."

The unresolved question of whether the wound inflicted at Borodino was mortal had hung over Kutuzov's head for an entire month. On the one hand, the French had occupied Moscow. On the other, Kutuzov felt certain with his whole being that the terrible blow into which he and all of Russia had poured their strength must have been fatal. But he needed proof. He had waited a whole month and was growing more impatient every day. Lying on his bed during those sleepless nights, he did exactly what he criticized the younger generals for doing: he imagined every possible scenario. But unlike them, he saw thousands of possibilities instead of two or three, and based nothing on any of them. He imagined every conceivable movement of Napoleon's army—as a whole or in parts—against Petersburg, or against him, or to outflank him. He also considered the possibility he feared most: that Napoleon might turn his own weapon against him and simply stay in Moscow, waiting him out. Kutuzov even imagined the French army turning back through Medyn and Yukhnov. But the one thing he could not foresee was what actually happened: the insane, convulsive stampede of Napoleon's army during its first eleven days after leaving Moscow—a stampede that made possible what Kutuzov hadn't yet dared to imagine: the complete destruction of the French. Dorokhov's report about Broussier's division, the guerrillas' reports of distress in Napoleon's army, and rumors of preparations to leave Moscow all supported the idea that the French army was beaten and preparing to flee. But these were only suppositions, which seemed important to the younger men but not to Kutuzov. With his sixty years of experience, he knew the value of rumors, knew how readily people who want something will arrange all the news to confirm their wishes, and ignore everything that contradicts them. The more he wanted to believe, the less he allowed himself to. This question consumed all his mental energy. Everything else was mere routine—his conversations with the staff, his letters to Madame de Staël, his reading of novels, the distribution of awards, his correspondence with Petersburg, and so on. But the destruction of the French, which he alone foresaw, was his heart's one desire.
On the night of the eleventh of October, he lay propped on his arm, thinking about it.
There was movement in the next room, and he heard the footsteps of Toll, Konovnitsyn, and Bolkhovitinov.
"Hello—who's there? Come in, come in! What news?" the field marshal called out.
While a servant lit a candle, Toll communicated the substance of the news.
"Who brought it?" asked Kutuzov, and when the candle was lit, Toll was struck by the cold severity of his expression.
"There can be no doubt about it, Your Highness."
"Call him in. Bring him here."

Kutuzov sat up with one leg hanging off the bed and his large belly resting against the other leg, which was doubled under him. He squinted his seeing eye to scrutinize the messenger more carefully, as if trying to read in his face what occupied his own mind.

"Tell me, tell me, my friend," he said to Bolkhovitinov in his low, aged voice, pulling together the shirt that gaped open on his chest. "Come closer—closer. What news have you brought? Napoleon has left Moscow? Are you sure?"
Bolkhovitinov gave a detailed account of everything he had been told to report.
"Speak faster, faster! Don't torture me!" Kutuzov interrupted.

Bolkhovitinov told him everything and fell silent, awaiting orders. Toll started to say something, but Kutuzov stopped him. He tried to speak himself, but his face suddenly crumpled and wrinkled. He waved his arm at Toll and turned to the opposite side of the room, toward the corner darkened by the icons hanging there.
"O Lord, my Creator, You have heard our prayer..." he said in a trembling voice, with folded hands. "Russia is saved. I thank You, O Lord!" And he wept.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: From the moment he received this news until the end of the campaign, all of Kutuzov's energy was directed toward restraining his troops—by authority, by cunning, and by pleading—from useless attacks, maneuvers, and clashes with the dying enemy. Dokhturov went to Malo-Yaroslavets, but Kutuzov lingered with the main army and gave orders for the evacuation of Kaluga—a retreat beyond that town seemed entirely possible to him.
Everywhere Kutuzov retreated, but the enemy, without waiting for his retreat, fled in the opposite direction.

Napoleon's historians describe his skillful maneuvers at Tarutino and Malo-Yaroslavets and speculate about what might have happened if Napoleon had managed to reach the rich southern provinces in time.

But setting aside the fact that nothing prevented him from advancing south (the Russian army wasn't blocking his way), the historians forget that nothing could have saved his army, because it already carried within itself the seeds of inevitable destruction. How could that army—which had found abundant supplies in Moscow and trampled them underfoot instead of preserving them, and which on arriving at Smolensk had looted provisions instead of storing them—how could such an army recover in Kaluga province, inhabited by the same kind of Russians who lived in Moscow, where fire had the same ability to consume whatever was set ablaze?
That army could not recover anywhere. Since the Battle of Borodino and the pillaging of Moscow, it had carried within itself the chemical elements of its own dissolution.

The members of what had once been an army—Napoleon himself and all his soldiers—fled without knowing where, each concerned only with escaping as quickly as possible from a situation whose hopelessness they all more or less vaguely sensed.

So at the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, when the generals pretended to deliberate and offered various opinions, all mouths were shut by the opinion of the plain-spoken soldier Mouton, who spoke last and said what they all felt: the only thing to do was get away as fast as possible. And no one—not even Napoleon—could argue against that truth they all recognized.

But though everyone realized they had to retreat, there remained a feeling of shame at admitting they had to flee. An outside jolt was needed to overcome that shame, and it came right on time. The French called it 'the Emperor's hurrah.'

The day after the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, Napoleon rode out early among the lines of his army with his marshals and escort, ostensibly to inspect the troops and the scene of the recent and upcoming battle. Some Cossacks out looking for plunder ran into the Emperor and very nearly captured him. What saved Napoleon wasn't the strength of his forces but the very thing that was destroying the French army: the lure of loot. The Cossacks went after the plunder, just as they had at Tarutino, leaving the men behind. Ignoring Napoleon, they chased the booty, and Napoleon managed to escape.

When 'the children of the Don' could so easily have captured the Emperor himself in the midst of his army, it was clear there was nothing to do but flee as fast as possible along the nearest, most familiar road. Napoleon, with his forty-year-old stomach, understood the hint. No longer feeling his former agility and boldness, and shaken by the fright the Cossacks had given him, he immediately agreed with Mouton and issued orders—as the historians tell us—to retreat along the Smolensk road.

That Napoleon agreed with Mouton, and that the army retreated, doesn't prove that Napoleon caused it to retreat. Rather, the forces influencing the entire army and directing it along the Mozhaysk (that is, the Smolensk) road were simultaneously acting on him as well.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: A person in motion always invents a purpose for that motion. To be able to march a thousand miles, you must believe that something good awaits you at the end of those thousand miles. You need the prospect of a promised land to have the strength to keep moving.

For the French during their advance, the promised land had been Moscow. During their retreat, it was their homeland. But their homeland was too far away, and for someone traveling a thousand miles, it's absolutely necessary to set aside the final goal and tell yourself: 'Today I'll reach a place twenty-five miles ahead, where I'll rest for the night.' And during that first day's march, the resting place eclipses the ultimate destination and draws all your hopes and desires. The impulses felt by a single person are always magnified in a crowd.

For the French retreating along the old Smolensk road, the final goal—their homeland—was too remote. Their immediate goal was Smolensk, toward which all their desires and hopes, enormously intensified in the mass, propelled them onward. It wasn't that they knew plenty of food and fresh troops awaited them in Smolensk, nor were they told so (on the contrary, their officers and Napoleon himself knew that provisions there were scarce). But this was the only thing that could give them the strength to keep moving and endure their present suffering. So those who knew and those who didn't both deceived themselves and pushed on toward Smolensk as toward a promised land.

Reaching the highway, the French fled with astonishing energy and unheard-of speed toward their chosen goal. Besides the shared impulse that bound the entire French mass into one body and gave it a kind of energy, there was another force holding them together: their sheer numbers. As with the physical law of gravity, their enormous mass drew individual human atoms to itself. In their hundreds of thousands, they moved like an entire nation.

Each man wanted nothing more than to give himself up as a prisoner and escape the horror and misery. But on one hand, the gravitational pull of Smolensk drew every one of them in the same direction; on the other, an army corps can't surrender to a company. Though the French seized every opportunity to break away and surrender on the slightest decent pretext, such opportunities didn't always arise. Their very numbers and the speed of their movement made it not just difficult but impossible for the Russians to halt them. No mechanical force could hasten the process of decomposition beyond a certain point.
A lump of snow can't be melted all at once. There is a minimum time required, and no amount of heat can melt it faster. In fact, the more heat you apply, the harder the remaining snow becomes.

Of the Russian commanders, Kutuzov alone understood this. When the French army's flight along the Smolensk road became well established, what Konovnitsyn had foreseen on the night of the eleventh began to happen. Every senior officer wanted to distinguish himself—to cut off, seize, capture, and crush the French—and all clamored for action.
Kutuzov alone used all his power (and a commander in chief's power is very limited) to prevent an attack.

He couldn't tell them what we can say now: 'Why fight? Why block the road, losing our own men and inhumanely slaughtering miserable wretches? What's the point, when a third of their army has already melted away on the march from Moscow to Vyazma without a single battle?' But drawing on his years of wisdom, he told them what they could understand—about the golden bridge—and they laughed at him and slandered him, flinging themselves on, tearing at, and gloating over the dying beast.

Ermolov, Miloradovich, Platov, and others near the French at Vyazma couldn't resist their desire to cut off and smash two French corps. To inform Kutuzov of their intentions, they sent him a blank sheet of paper in an envelope.

And try as Kutuzov might to hold the troops back, the Russians attacked, trying to block the road. Infantry regiments, we are told, advanced with music playing and drums beating, and killed and lost thousands of men.
But they didn't cut off or capture anyone. The French army, closing ranks more tightly in the face of danger, continued to melt steadily away as it pursued its fatal path toward Smolensk.
